definition: A property of particles such as electrons (negative) and protons (positive) that makes them push or pull on each other through electric and magnetic fields.
A physical quantity with a value (and usually a direction) at every point in space, such as the electric or magnetic field.
The force a small test charge would feel at a point, divided by its charge (E = F/q). Measured in N/C, equivalent to V/m.
The field created by moving charges (currents) that pushes on other moving charges. Measured in teslas (T).
A self-sustaining oscillation of electric and magnetic fields that travels through space at the speed of light. It is launched by accelerating charges.
A charge that is speeding up, slowing down or changing direction. Only accelerating charges radiate EM waves.
A wave whose oscillation is perpendicular to its direction of travel. In an EM wave, both E and B are perpendicular to the direction of travel.
An idealized wave whose crests are flat planes, a good model for light far from its source.
The speed of all EM waves in vacuum: exactly 299,792,458 m/s, rounded to 3.00 × 10^8 m/s in this book.
The distance between neighboring crests of a wave, in meters.
The number of wave cycles passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz = 1/s). Related to wavelength by c = λf.
The time for one full oscillation at a fixed point; T = 1/f.
The peak strength of a wave's electric field, in V/m. It sets the wave's brightness, not its color.
The power a wave delivers per unit area, in W/m². For an EM wave, I = ½cε0E0², so intensity grows as amplitude squared.
The direction in which a wave's electric field oscillates.
Light whose electric field direction is a random, rapidly changing mix of all directions perpendicular to the beam, such as sunlight or bulb light.
A material that transmits only the component of the electric field along its transmission axis and absorbs the perpendicular component.
For polarized light hitting a polarizer whose axis is at angle θ to the light's polarization, the transmitted intensity is I = I0 cos²θ.
The angle of incidence at which reflected light is completely polarized parallel to the surface; about 53° from the vertical for water.
A conductor in which electrons are driven back and forth to launch EM waves, or are driven by arriving waves to detect them.
